items.title: Trump's ICE Sent Thousands of Recruits Out After Training Them Online
items.author: Andre Costa
items.content:
The Trump regime let more than 3,500 ICE recruits skip a month of in-person training and do their basic training online instead, a 19-page draft report by the Department of Homeland Security's inspector general found. More than 80% of them finished the online modules within ten days, more than 10% in under 24 hours and at least five in about two hours. The New York Times obtained the draft, which has not been finalised or made public, on Friday.

The recruits who did their training online all had previous law enforcement experience, and they were part of nearly 6,000 officers who got reduced training between August 2025 and July 2026.

ICE cut academy instruction for more than 2,000 recruits with no police background from about 543 hours to roughly 300, taking hours from firearms, arrest procedures and driving. It also scrapped the two-attempt limit on a training test, and one officer needed 32 attempts to pass. Nearly 90% of the ICE officials running on-the-job training who answered the watchdog's questionnaire said that training was "not successful", and one ICE instructor called the overhaul a "catastrophic failure".

Kristi Noem, then Homeland Security Secretary, and her senior adviser Corey Lewandowski strongly backed the changes, and ICE's former training chief told investigators he was ordered to make them. Trump ousted Noem in March. Her successor, Markwayne Mullin, restored stricter requirements in July, but the draft says ICE "has not fully addressed training gaps born of the reductions and revisions" for the officers it had already sent out.

The shortcuts fed the regime's hiring drive for its mass deportation campaign. ICE announced on 3 January that it had hired more than 12,000 officers and agents in under a year, more than doubling its force from about 10,000 to 22,000, paid for with $8 billion from Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act and $50,000 signing bonuses. On 22 January the department claimed that all new ICE students attend the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center and "meet the same high standards ICE has always required". More than 3,500 of them were doing it online.

ICE officer David Brouillette was one of the experienced hires. He joined late in 2025 and on 13 July shot dead Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian father with a pending asylum case and a work permit, during a vehicle stop in Biddeford, Maine. Guerrero was not the man ICE had a warrant for. Because Brouillette had worked as a police officer at a Veterans Affairs medical centre, ICE skipped him past the training centre and gave him a virtual course followed by field use-of-force training. Two former wives have accused him of abuse, a Maine judge ordered him to give up his guns in 2019, and he denies the allegations. Maine has not charged him.

Federal agents in Minneapolis shot dead Renee Good, a 37-year-old mother, on 7 January, and Alex Pretti, an intensive care nurse, on 24 January, both of them US citizens. ICE and CBP had killed or let die 97 people since January 2025 by the end of October, a count the Crust News team keeps on the ICE List at theicelist.org. The draft did not examine whether the training cuts played a part in any of those deaths.

Inspector General Joseph Cuffari's office condemned the release of the draft, saying such disclosures "undermine the integrity of the oversight process". ICE said "a significant portion of officers brought on during the hiring surge have law enforcement experience and have already successfully completed a law enforcement academy". Mullin told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday that "there were some decisions that were made before I was secretary that we are having to undo".

The draft says ICE has still not closed the training gaps left in the thousands of officers it hired under Noem's rules.

items.title: ICE List Confirms the Identities of 5,000 Immigration Agents
items.author: Andre Costa
items.content:
ICE List has confirmed the identities of more than 5,000 immigration agents, more than double the roughly 2,200 on our public record on 28 October, the day a staff directory of the Department of Homeland Security was leaked.

The leak, is available to the public via the transparency group DDoSecrets under the name Icepick, holds 41,191 records of DHS employees and contractors. A group calling itself the Department of Peace says it took them through the single sign-on service DHS buys from Okta. Okta says it has "no evidence our data or systems were compromised". DHS said it was "aware of a potential breach".

A name in the leak does not get anyone onto ICE List. The leak tells us where to look, and a page goes up only when we can tie the name to an agent through a source outside it, such as a court filing, an official record or press reporting. About 2,270 of the named agents on the record are documented in court filings, most of them filed by the government itself.

Crucially, a number of the people named in the leak no longer work at ICE, and some have retired. The directory covers the whole department, with 21,329 records from Customs and Border Protection and 6,598 from ICE, and it is a list of accounts, which is a different thing from a list of the people making arrests today.

Those who have moved on from the agency show the crucial need for a steady hand with information like this. The ICE List is targeted at the Trump regime's transformation of ICE and Border Patrol, and many of those who left as soon as Trump took charge may indeed oppose the tactics that are now commonplace.

For now we are working only through the field agents. We will go through the remaining names afterwards to see whether any have joined ICE or CBP since.

More than 20 of the names we have confirmed were searched for on our site from DHS and ICE work computers. Our logs record the network a search comes from and cannot show who typed it. They do show that somebody inside the department went looking for those names on ICE List before we had published them. DHS's own network sent more than 10,000 requests to the site in the two weeks to 29 October.

We do not publish home addresses, phone numbers or email addresses. This is a common claim by opponents of our project, and indeed, by the US government itself. As confirmed by multiple investigations, no addresses appear on the ICE List.

ICE agents make arrests in masks, in plain clothes and from unmarked cars, and the Trump regime refuses to name them even after they have shot someone. DHS says naming agents puts them and their families in danger. The agents on this record are public officials using the powers of the state in public, and in most cases the government has already named them in a courtroom.

Every page lists its sources. Anyone who believes they have been named in error can contact us and we will check the record against the evidence. Footage, documents and names can be sent to the same place.

ICE Watch, the app the public uses to send footage, photos and plate numbers to ICE List, is now in testing on Google Play. Join the test to install it on your phone.

ICE List and Crust News are paid for by readers. Subscribe to get our reporting by email, or donate to keep the record growing.

items.title: Bringing the Largest Public ICE Database to Your Phone
items.author: Dominick Skinner
items.content:
After months of rejections, the ICE Watch app has been accepted onto the Google Play store, and we can now invite testers to join and help get the app approved for a full release. Many people will not want to install the app through the store, and the .apk install is still available at its old location. The Play Store will not replace the third party routes.

We will pursue an iPhone version as soon as the app passes through the testing period on Android.

ICE Watch is the app that lets the public contribute to The ICE List. It has had limited use so far because we could not get it approved for the official Android app store.

On November 13, a US federal judge issued a permanent injunction barring the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security from pressuring Apple and Meta to suppress platforms used to monitor ICE activity. That injunction is the reason we chose now to resubmit the app to the Play Store, and may be the reason it was accepted.

Google puts a new app through a closed test before it can go onto the store for everyone. A set of testers has to install it and keep it for two weeks before anyone else can. We need those testers now.

The app has been in use for five months, so this is early access more than a test.

With the app you can swipe through documented ICE operations and the agents nobody has named yet, Tinder-style, and help identify the agents we have not been able to.

The full ICE List is in the app too. Browse by state, and send footage or a tip from your phone in seconds. Share a video from your gallery straight to us. Nothing you send appears publicly until a person has reviewed it, and tips are anonymous.

We made one serious change for the Google Play version: logins are gone. Anyone who installs from the Play Store gets an anonymous ID. This makes no real difference to most users, but the groups who work alongside us have been asked to install from the F-Droid store or the .apk file instead.

If you want to help test it, leave the email of a Google account on your phone at blog.theicelist.org/testers. We will send you a link to install the app. Keep it for three weeks, use it as you would anyway, and tell us what, if anything, breaks at icelist@crustnews.com.

If you use an iPhone, you do not have to wait for the iOS app. Open watch.theicelist.org in Safari, tap the Share button at the bottom of the screen, then tap Add to Home Screen. ICE Watch then opens from your home screen like any other app, full screen, and you can send footage and tips from it the same way.

The ICE List takes no advertising and no institutional money. It is funded by the public. If you want to help this project grow, please consider supporting it here.
